p.seg: Chūnqiū Fánlù Volume 1
"Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng First"
"Chǔ Zhuāng Wáng killed Chén Xià Zhēngshū,
the *Chūnqiū* devalued the writing about it,
not granting it a special discussion;
Líng Wáng killed Qí Qìngfēng,
and directly called him 'Chǔ Zǐ',
why?"
He said:
"Zhuāng Wáng's actions were virtuous,
and Zhēngshū's crimes were serious.
When a virtuous ruler punishes a serious crime,
it is good in the eyes of the people.
If it were not devalued,
who would know that it was not orthodox?
The *Chūnqiū* always uses cases where one seems to be gaining something improperly
to show their lack of propriety.
Therefore, Qí Huán was not granted a special territory to enfeoff,
Jìn Wén was not granted the authority to bring a king to audience and court,
Chǔ Zhuāng was not granted the authority to specially kill and punish.
If these three were not allowed,
then the attainments of the feudal lords,
would almost be diminished!
This is why Chǔ Líng was called 'Zǐ' when he carried out the punishment.
The language of the *Chūnqiū* is often allegorical,
its writing is concise, but its rules are clear."
Someone asked:
"The fact that the feudal lords were not allowed to make exclusive enfeoffments is
demonstrated again by the destruction of Chén and Cài.
The fact that the feudal lords were not allowed to make exclusive punitive expeditions,
why is this not demonstrated again by the killing by Qìng Fēng?
Why is that?"
He replied:
"The use of language in the *Spring and Autumn Annals* is such that
what is already clear is omitted,
and what is not clear is recorded.
Now, the fact that the feudal lords are not allowed to make exclusive punitive expeditions
is already clear.
However, Qìng Fēng's crime has not been shown,
therefore, it refers to the Viscount of Chǔ using his hegemonic position to punish him,
recording that his crime deserved death,
to establish a great prohibition for the world.
It says:
the actions of a subject,
which degrade the position of the lord,
and the ministers who cause chaos in the state,
even if they do not usurp and kill,
their crimes all deserve death.
Compared to this,
that is the reason."
"The *Spring and Autumn Annals* says:
'Jìn attacked Xiān Yú.'
Why does it consider Jìn evil and equate it with the barbarian Di tribes?"
Said:
"The *Chūnqiū* (
Trust is valued more than land,
and ritual is honored more than one's own person.
How do we know this is so?
Sòng Bójī (宋伯姬) feared impropriety and died in the fire;
Qí Huángōng (齊桓公) suspected trust and diminished his land.
The *Chūnqiū* deemed them virtuous and recorded them,
as models for the world.
To speak of ritual and trust,
no ritual will go unanswered,
and no act of generosity will go unreturned;
this is the way of Heaven.
Now my ruler and minister, being of the same surname, marry off a daughter.
The daughter has no conscience,
so the ritual receives no response.
There is fear that they might fear me;
how is this not barbarian-like!
During the rebellion of Gōngzǐ Qìngfù (公子慶父),
Lǔ (魯) was in grave danger of annihilation,
yet Qí Huángōng (齊桓公) secured it.
He had no familial connection to them,
yet he still came to worry about us.
How can you, being of the same surname, treat us with such cruelty and violence?
The *Shī* (*Classic of Poetry*, 詩) says:
'Look at that cooing dove,
its wings flying up to Heaven.
My heart is saddened,
Thinking of those ancestors.
At daybreak I cannot sleep,
my heart cherishes those two men."
All men have this feeling.
Now Jìn is not worried about me because we share the same surname,
but because it is strong, it is repulsed by me,
and my heart is disappointed.
Therefore, when the words are not good,
saying only "It's Jìn,"
is a euphemism."
The questioner said:
"Jìn is wicked and cannot be approached,
you went but dared not arrive,
this is only human nature.
Why would a *jūnzǐ* be ashamed and claim to be ill?"
He replied:
"Evil comes without reason,
a *jūnzǐ* is not ashamed.
Introspecting and finding no fault,
what worry, what fear?
That is all.
Now, the *Chūnqiū* shames those [who are ashamed],
*Zhāo Gōng* had reason to incur it.
Ministers overstep their rulers,
beginning with *Wén* and becoming extreme with *Zhāo*.
The duke received a chaotic decline,
and had no heart of fear or alertness,
Acting rashly and lightly planning reckless attacks,
violating great propriety by marrying someone of the same surname,
and embracing injustice while heavily degrading oneself.
People say:
"When a state is well-governed,
the neighboring states congratulate it;
when a state is in turmoil,
the neighboring states scatter."
Therefore, Jì Sūn monopolized his position,
and the major states did not rectify him.
He fled for eight years,
and only after his death was he allowed to return.
He himself perished and his son was endangered,
the height of misfortune.
A gentleman is not ashamed of his hardship,
but is ashamed of the reason for his impoverishment.
Although Zhāo Gōng encountered this time,
if he had not married someone of the same surname,
how could he have reached this point?
Even if he had married someone of the same surname,
if he had been able to employ Kǒngzǐ to assist him,
he would also not have reached this point.
The times were difficult but governance was simple,
and he acted perversely without rescue;
this is the reason for his impoverishment."
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* divides twelve generations into three categories:
those witnessed,
There are those seen,
there are those heard about.
Those seen, span three generations;
those heard about, four generations;
those passed down by hearsay, five generations.
Therefore, (the events during the reigns of) Duke Āi, Duke Dìng, Duke Zhāo,
are what the gentleman personally witnessed.
(The events during the reigns of) Duke Xiāng, Duke Chéng, Duke Wén, Duke Xuān,
are what the gentleman heard about.
(The events during the reigns of) Duke Xī, Duke Mǐn, Duke Zhuāng, Duke Huán, Duke Yǐn,
are what the gentleman learned of through hearsay.
Those seen, cover sixty-one years;
those heard about, eighty-five years;
those learned by hearsay, ninety-six years.
Regarding those seen,
the words are subtle;
regarding those heard about,
the calamities are lamented;
regarding those learned by hearsay,
the favors are suppressed;
all accord with feelings.
Therefore, in expelling the Jì clan and speaking of holding another *yú* sacrifice,
the words are subtle.
Zǐ Chì was killed,
(and) it could not be borne to record the day,
the calamities are lamented.
Zǐ Bān was killed,
and recorded as *yǐ wèi*,
It eliminates the kindness toward them.
The intention to yield and stretch,
the detailed and concise writing,
all respond to it.
I believe that it treats those near as near and those far as far, those who are close as close and those who are distant as distant,
and also understands that it values the valued and despises the despised, weighs the heavy and light,
and also understands that it treats the generous as generous and the stingy as stingy, the good as good and the evil as evil,
and also understands that it treats the bright as bright and the dark as dark, the white as white and the black as black.
All things have pairs,
pair them and unite them,
match the enemies and pair them,
good!
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Dignified and restrained,
virtuous words orderly,
without resentment or wickedness,
following the ranks of peers."
This is what it means.
Therefore, the *Spring and Autumn Annals* is the greatest of righteousness;
grasp one end and understand it broadly;
observe its right and wrong,
and you can obtain its correct method;
observe its gentle words,
and you can know how to stop resentment.
Therefore, externally,
it speaks of the Way but does not make it obvious;
internally,
it conceals but does not hide completely;
It is the same with respect for superiors;
It is the same with respect for the worthy;
This is how one distinguishes between inner and outer, differentiates between the worthy and the unworthy, and equalizes the honored and the humble.
Righteousness does not slander superiors,
Wisdom does not endanger oneself,
Therefore, those far away conceal through righteousness,
Those nearby are awed by wisdom,
When awe and righteousness are combined,
then as the generation gets closer, speech becomes more cautious.
This is why the words of Duke Dìng and Duke Āi were subtle.
Therefore, if it is applied, the world is at peace;
if it is not applied, one secures one's own person;
this is the Dao of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
The Dao of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*
Reveres Heaven and models itself on antiquity.
Therefore, even with skillful hands,
if one does not follow the compass and square,
one cannot correct squares and circles;
even with discerning ears,
if one does not play the six pitch-pipes,
one cannot determine the five tones;
even with a wise heart,
if one does not examine the former kings,
one cannot bring peace to the world.
Then, the way left behind by the former kings,
is indeed the compass, square, and pitch-pipes of the world!
Therefore, the sages model themselves on Heaven,
The wise emulate the sages,
this is the great principle;
obtain the great principle and there is order,
lose the great principle and there is chaos,
this is the distinction between order and chaos;
it is said that under Heaven there are not two paths,
therefore the sages have different governance but the same principle,
they are thoroughly versed in the past and present,
therefore the former sages transmitted their methods to later generations.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals*'s relationship to world affairs
is that it excels at restoring the ancient ways,
and it censures changing the norm,
desiring to emulate the methods of the former kings.
However, it is introduced with one statement, saying:
"A king must change institutions."
The self-willed obtain this as an excuse,
saying:
"If the past could be followed,
why did the ways of the former kings not continue to follow one another?"
The world is confused by hearing this,
and doubts the correct path while believing in heretical words,
which is deeply concerning.
I answer them, saying:
"There was a man who heard that the lords of the feudal states enjoyed the music of 'Shooting the Leopard Head,'
so he cut off a leopard's head himself,
hung it up and shot at it,
saying:
'Where is the enjoyment in this?'
This is hearing the name without knowing the reality.
What is now called the new king necessarily changing the system,
is not changing the Way,
is not altering the principle.
Receiving the Mandate from Heaven,
changing the surname and replacing the king,
is not succeeding the former king to rule.
If one merely follows the previous system,
cultivates the old affairs,
and has nothing changed,
then there is no way to distinguish it from succeeding the former king to rule.
The ruler who receives the Mandate,
is what Heaven greatly reveals.
Serving a father is to inherit his intentions,
serving a ruler is to model his will,
serving Heaven is also the same.
Now, if Heaven greatly reveals itself,
and things inherit what has been replaced and generally remain the same,
then it is neither revealing nor clear,
and is not the will of Heaven.
Therefore, one must move residences, change titles, reform the calendar, and change clothing colors;
there is no other reason,
than daring not to disobey the will of Heaven and to clearly reveal oneself.
If the great principles, human relationships, doctrines, politics, teachings, customs, and literary meanings are all as before,
then what is there to change?
Therefore, a king has the name of changing the system,
but not the reality of changing the Way.
Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) said:
"He who governs by non-action,
is it not Shùn!"
This speaks only of the way of his lord Yáo,
is this not the effect of no change!"
The questioner said:
"Things change and Heaven bestows,
it is clear,
but why must new music be made?"
What is the reason?"
He replied:
"Music is different from this.
Institutions are made in response to heavenly changes,
music is made in response to human changes.
Those who receive the mandate
must share joy with the people.
Therefore, great changes in institutions are made at the beginning,
to clarify the mandate of Heaven;
the making of new music is done at the end,
to display the accomplishment of Heaven;
based on what the world newly delights in, one creates musical compositions,
to harmonize the government
and to promote virtue,
before the world is universally in harmony,
the ruler does not make music in vain.
Music is that which is full within and moves and emanates outwards,
responding to the time of governance,
establishing rites and making music to complete it,
completion means that the fundamental, the subsidiary, the substance, and the ornamentation are all complete.
Therefore, those who create music must always look back to what the world initially found pleasing, taking their own pleasure as the foundation.
In the time of Shùn,
the people rejoiced in his making Yáo's achievements manifest,
hence the music called "Sháo."
"Sháo" means to manifest;
in the time of Yǔ,
the people rejoiced that three sages succeeded one another,
hence the music called "Xià."
"Xià" means great;
in the time of Tāng,
the people rejoiced that he rescued them from calamity and harm,
hence the music called "Hù."
"Hù" means rescue;
in the time of King Wén,
the people rejoiced in his raising armies and launching conquests,
hence the music called "Wǔ."
"Wǔ" means conquest.
These four were universally enjoyed throughout the world,
and were one and the same
but the reasons for this common joy
are not the same.
The method of creating music
must always revert to the source of what is pleasurable.
If what is pleasurable is not the same in each event,
how could the music not change from generation to generation!
Therefore, Shùn created "Sháo," and Yǔ created "Xià,"
Tāng created "Hù," and King Wén created "Wǔ."
These four pieces of music have different names
then each would obey his people, and begin to find joy in himself.
I have seen its effects.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"King Wén received the mandate,
and possessed such martial accomplishments;
having attacked Chóng,
he built the city of Fēng."
This is the style of *lè* (music).
It also says:
"The King was greatly angered,
and then mustered his troops."
At that time,
Zhòu was without the proper Way,
the feudal lords were in great disarray,
and the people rejoiced at the anger of King Wén and sang of it.
The virtue of the people of Zhōu had already reached all under heaven,
they returned to the root as their joy,
and called it "The Great Martial (Dà Wǔ),"
saying that what the people initially rejoiced in was martial prowess, that is all.
Therefore, generally, with all music,
it is created at the end,
but named by its beginning,
emphasizing the meaning of the root.
Viewed from this,
changes in the calendar and official clothing,
the differences in receiving the mandate, responding to heaven, establishing rites, and creating music,
are all movements of the human heart,
these two separate but then reunite,
What is done is the same."
"Jade Cup, Number Two"
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* criticized Duke Wén for marrying during the mourning period.
The challenger said:
"The rules of mourning,
do not exceed three years;
the three years of mourning,
is twenty-five months.
Now, according to the *Classic*,
Duke Wén married after forty-one months,
when he married, there was no mourning.
It had long been outside the rules;
why call it marrying during mourning?"
He replied:
"'The Spring and Autumn Annals' in discussing matters,
places the greatest importance on intention.
Now, marriage inevitably involves offering betrothal gifts,
and the month of offering betrothal gifts fell within the mourning period.
Therefore, it is called marrying during mourning.
Furthermore, Duke Wén performed the autumn *xiá* sacrifice
and offered betrothal gifts in winter.
Both were excessively early.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* does not criticize what came before,
but only criticizes what came after.
Certainly, the three years of mourning,
is a matter of heartfelt emotion.
Even if one follows custom and cannot complete it,
猶宜未平於心， [yóu yí wèi píng yú xīn,] It would still be appropriate for his heart not to be at peace.
今全無悼遠之志， [jīn quán wú dào yuǎn zhī zhì,] But now he has no intention of mourning the deceased at all.
反思念娶事， [fǎn sīniàn qǔ shì,] On the contrary, he is thinking about the matter of taking a wife.
是《春秋》之所甚疾也， [shì "chūn qiū" zhī suǒ shèn jí yě,] This is what the *Spring and Autumn Annals* severely condemns.
故譏不出三年於首而已， [gù jī bù chū sān nián yú shǒu ér yǐ,] Therefore, it criticizes that he does not complete even the three years of mourning,
譏以喪娶也。 [jī yǐ sàng qǔ yě.] Criticizing him for marrying during mourning.
不別先後， [bù bié xiān hòu,] Not distinguishing between what should come first and what should come after,
賤其無人心也。 [jiàn qí wú rén xīn yě.] Devalues him for having no human feelings.
緣此以論禮， [yuán cǐ yǐ lùn lǐ,] Based on this to discuss ritual,
禮之所重者在其志， [lǐ zhī suǒ zhòng zhě zài qí zhì,] what ritual values is in one's intentions.
志敬而節具， [zhì jìng ér jié jù,] If one's intentions are reverent and the formalities are complete,
則君子予之知禮； [zé jūnzǐ yǔ zhī zhī lǐ;] then the gentleman will acknowledge that he understands ritual.
志和而音雅， [zhì hé ér yīn yǎ,] If one's intentions are harmonious and the music is refined,
則君子予之知樂； [zé jūnzǐ yǔ zhī zhī yuè;] then the gentleman will acknowledge that he understands music.
志哀而居約， [zhì āi ér jū yuē,] If one's intentions are mournful and one lives frugally,
則君子予之知喪。 [zé jūnzǐ yǔ zhī zhī sàng.] then the gentleman will acknowledge that he understands mourning.
故曰： [gù yuē:] Therefore it is said:
非虛加之， [fēi xū jiā zhī,] Not to add them emptily,
重志之謂也。 [zhòng zhì zhī wèi yě.] It is to value intentions.
志為質， [zhì wèi zhì,] Intention is the substance,
物為文， [wù wèi wén,] the outward forms are the ornamentation.
文著於質， [wén zhù yú zhì,] The ornamentation is manifested in the substance,
質不居文， [zhì bù jū wén,] If the substance does not dwell in the ornamentation,
文安施質； [wén ān shī zhì;] where shall the ornamentation be applied?
質文兩備， [zhì wén liǎng bèi,] When both substance and ornamentation are complete,
然後其禮成； [ránhòu qí lǐ chéng;] then the ritual is complete.
文質偏行， [wén zhì piān xíng,] If either ornamentation or substance is pursued alone,
不得有我爾之名； [bùdé yǒu wǒ ěr zhī míng;] neither you nor I will gain a good reputation.
When both cannot be fully achieved and one is prioritized,
it is better to have substance without embellishment.
Even if it doesn't quite reach the standard of propriety,
it is still somewhat virtuous.
The arrival of Jiè Gélú 介葛盧 is an example of this.
To have embellishment without substance
is not only not acceptable,
but even somewhat detestable.
The arrival of Zhōu Gōng Shí 州公寔 is an example of this.
Therefore, the order of priorities in the *Chūnqiū* 春秋 is to
value substance first and embellishment after,
prioritize intention on the right and material things on the left.
Therefore, it is said:
"Ritual, ritual!
Is it merely about jade and silk?"
Extend this forward,
and one should also say:
"Court audience, court audience!
Is it merely about words and speeches?"
"Music, music!
Is it merely about bells and drums?"
Draw this backward,
and one should also say:
"Mourning, mourning!
Is it merely about clothing?"
Therefore, Kǒngzǐ 孔子 established the Way of a new king,
clarifying that valuing intention leads to harmony,
and demonstrating that a fondness for sincerity eliminates hypocrisy.
"It is because it inherited the failings of Zhōu,
therefore it is like this."
The principle of the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) is:
to have the people follow the ruler,
and to have the ruler follow Heaven.
It says:
"Considering the hearts of the people and ministers,
there cannot be a day without a ruler,
(since) there cannot be a day without a ruler,
and yet (the heir) still calls himself 'son' for three years,
(this is) because the heart of the ruler has not yet been properly established,
is this not having the people follow the ruler!
The heart of a filial son
is not yet appropriate for three years.
(But) if he ascends the throne the year after the three years is over,
it is in accordance with the beginning and end of the cycle of Heaven,
is this not having the ruler follow Heaven!
Therefore, to subdue the people and exalt the ruler,
(and) to subdue the ruler and exalt Heaven,
is the great meaning of the *Chūnqiū*.
The *Chūnqiū* discusses the affairs of twelve generations,
the Way of Man is fully understood and the Way of the King is complete.
The principles are spread throughout the two hundred and forty-two years,
assisting each other as left and right,
in order to create elegance,
their arrangement is interspersed,
It is not merely imitating the ancients.
Therefore, those who discuss the *Spring and Autumn Annals*
should combine and understand it thoroughly,
trace its origins and seek its meaning,
compare its similar instances,
match its categories,
examine its underlying principles,
and remove its redundancies.
Thus, the way of humanity is pervasive and the laws of the king are established.
Do you think this is not the case?
Now, the Son of Heaven ascends the throne after a year,
and the feudal lords within their fiefs call themselves "son" for three years;
these are not in the *Classic*,
but the way they are handled is no different than if they were in the *Classic*.
It is not that there is no distinction;
there is something seen, and the *Classic* can accept those additions.
Therefore, those who can use comparison to connect categories and use distinction to handle redundancies
have greatly understood it.
People receive their mandate from Heaven,
and have the nature of loving good and hating evil.
It can be nurtured but not changed,
can be predicted but not removed,
like the physical body which can become fat or thin,
but cannot be transformed.
Therefore, even if there is supreme virtue,
one can, for the sake of the ruler and parent, tolerate their evil,
but one cannot, for the sake of the ruler and parent, cause them to have no evil.
The *Book* says:
"When the sovereign does not act as a sovereign,
he loses his reverence."
Serving one's parents is also like this;
both are the extremes of loyalty and filial piety.
How could anyone but the most virtuous be like this?
If the father does not act as a father, then the son will not act as a son;
if the ruler does not act as a ruler, then the minister will not act as a minister.
Duke Wén was unable to observe mourning,
did not offer sacrifices at the proper times,
reversed the order by not observing the three-year mourning period,
and even married during mourning,
marrying a woman from a *dàfū* family,
thereby debasing the ancestral temple,
throwing his ancestral lines into confusion,
and rebelling against his predecessors.
He had not a single small good quality,
but four or five great evils;
therefore, the feudal lords did not give him their allegiance,
and the *dàfū* would not serve him.
These are signs of being detested and the effects of not being a minister.
He was insulted abroad
and plundered within;
he was a ruler without authority.
Confucius said:
"The administration has fallen into the hands of the *dàfū* for four generations now."
He was probably referring to the time since Duke Wén.
The gentleman knows that those in positions of authority cannot subdue people through evil.
Therefore, he selects the Six Arts to cultivate and nourish them.
The *Book of Poetry* and the *Book of Documents* express their aspirations.
The *Book of Rites* and the *Book of Music* purify their beauty.
The *Book of Changes* and the *Spring and Autumn Annals* illuminate their knowledge.
All six disciplines are grand,
and each has its strength.
The *Book of Poetry* speaks of aspiration,
therefore it excels in substance;
the *Book of Rites* establishes propriety,
therefore it excels in refinement;
the *Book of Music* praises virtue,
therefore it excels in influence;
the *Book of Documents* records achievements,
therefore it excels in matters of fact;
the *Book of Changes* is rooted in heaven and earth,
therefore it excels in numbers;
the *Spring and Autumn Annals* rectifies right and wrong,
therefore it excels in governing people;
one can obtain their respective strengths,
but one cannot exhaustively enumerate their details.
Therefore, if a ruler focuses solely on the grand principles, his wisdom will be obscured;
if he is overly broad in his learning, his endeavors will become weary.
These two represent different errors but lead to the same condemnation,
and the harm they cause will inevitably occur;
one must not fail to examine them.
Therefore, a good teacher
Since (one) admires its Dao,
one should be cautious in its practice.
Regulate the timing of early and late (activities),
bear the amount of much and little,
accommodate fast and slow (pace),
achieve without rushing,
examine without distress,
reflect on what one does,
and complete what one is absorbed in.
Therefore, strength is not taxed,
and the person is greatly accomplished.
This is called sage transformation;
I take it as my model.
Is the excellence of the *Spring and Autumn Annals* subtle?
It values the intent.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* cultivates the meaning of beginning and end,
comprehends the response to change and contingency,
penetrates the intention regarding life and death,
and fulfills the ultimate of human virtue.
Therefore, if the ruler is killed and the thief is punished,
then it is good to record their execution;
if no one punishes them,
then the ruler's burial is not recorded,
and the thief is not seen again.
Not recording the burial
is to indicate that there are no subjects and sons;
the thief not being seen again
Because it was fitting that it should be extinguished and cut off.
Now Zhào Dùn assassinated the ruler,
and four years later,
a separate entry was again recorded,
which is not the usual language of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
Scholars, past and present, differ and ask about it,
saying:
"This is an assassination of the ruler,
why is it recorded again?"
"It is like saying the rebels have not been punished,
why is a funeral recorded?
The reason a funeral is recorded,
is because it was not fitting to record a funeral, yet a funeral was recorded;
the reason it is recorded again,
is because it was not fitting to record it again, yet it was recorded again;
the two are connected by the same principle,
and cannot but be similar.
That Dùn was recorded again,
was simply to address the question and defend himself that he did not personally commit the assassination,
but it does not mean he should not be punished;
then one also cannot but say that the recording of Dào Gōng's funeral,
was simply to address the question and defend that the assassination was not completed,
and should not be blamed either.
If this is so, then the interpretation of the *Spring and Autumn Annals* is chaotic,
how can it be a model?"
"Therefore, to connect and compare in order to discuss right and wrong,
although it is difficult to fully grasp,
the principle is the same.
Now, to execute Dùn without precedent,
or not to execute without precedent,
to discuss it by analogy [with other cases],
is to argue according to the law;

Duke Huán of Lǔ forgot his worries,

Duke Huán of Qí worried about his worries,

Extrapolating and extending this,

those who have worries and deeply worry about them are fortunate.
The *Book of Changes* says:
"Returning from the Way,

This is what it means.
It is still difficult for a common man to turn away from the wrong path in order to remove blame,

The "Book of Poetry" says:
"Virtue is as light as a feather."
This speaks of its ease.
"The Duke watched fish at the pond,

"The nature of all people

Therefore, a gentleman never speaks of profit all day long,
wanting only to shame them by not speaking of it,
shaming them in order to block its source.
Those who are in positions to influence customs and transform people,
even just speaking the name of profit,
still detest it,
how much more so seeking profit!
Therefore, when the heavenly king sends people to seek funeral contributions and gold,
it is all recorded as a great evil.
Now it is not just sending people,
but seeking it personally,
which is an extremely great evil.
Why is it criticized as 'watching fish'?
It is the same as saying 'watching the community sacrifice',

The *Chūnqiū* has standard rituals,
and it has adapted rituals.
Things like maintaining a peaceful nature and a calm heart are standard rituals;
as for cases where:
although one's nature is not at peace,
and although one's heart is not calm,
yet there is no way to change the Dao,
these are adapted rituals.
Therefore, in wedding ceremonies, not addressing the host is a standard ritual;
standard ritual indeed;
when the excuses are exhausted and there is nothing else to call him,
addressing him as the host
is an adapted ritual.
The Son of Heaven only assumes the title of King after three years,
which is a standard ritual;
but if there is a contingency,
then he assumes the title of King before three years,
which is an adapted ritual.
Women do not have affairs outside of the borders,
this is a standard ritual;
but when a mother marries a wife for her son,
or rushes to the funeral of her parents,
these are adapted rituals.
Understanding the matters of standard and adapted rituals,
then one knows the divisions of importance and weight,
and can appropriately adapt to circumstances.
A questioner says:
"In the *Chūnqiū*, when events are the same, the language is the same.
These four instances are all cases of deviating from ritual propriety,
yet some accord with the classics,
while others do not.
Why is this?"
He replied:
"The *Chūnqiū* [Spring and Autumn Annals] governs all things,
distinguishes categories,
differentiates subtle nuances,
and cultivates the root and the branch.
Therefore, a falling star is called 'yǔn' (隕, meteor),
while locusts falling are called 'yǔ' (雨, rain).
Because the place from which they originate is different,
one descends from the sky,
the other arises from the earth,
their terminology cannot be the same.
Now, these four instances are all the same in that they are deviations from ritual propriety,
but the point of origin is also different,
some originate with men,
others originate with women,
so their terminology cannot be the same.
Therefore, some accord with the constant,
while others accord with the variable."

and hinders the teachings.
Teachings are the foundation of governance,
and judgments are the final aspect of governance;
their affairs are in different realms,
but their function is the same.
They must be mutually aligned,
therefore, the superior person values them greatly.
Someone who questioned the affairs of Jìn 晉 said:
"According to the principles of the *Chūnqiū* 春秋 [Spring and Autumn Annals],
a ruler who has not yet reigned for a full year is referred to as 'son' (zǐ 子).
This is the correctness of the human heart.
However, when Lì Kè 力克 assassinated Xī Qí 奚齊,
he avoided this correct term and called him 'son of the ruler' (jūn zhī zǐ 君之子).
Why is that?"
He said:
"I have heard that the *Book of Odes* has no definitive interpretations,
the *Book of Changes* has no definitive divinations,
and the *Spring and Autumn Annals* has no definitive wording.
They follow changes and follow righteousness,
and consistently serve people.
Benevolent people record the disasters of those of the same surname,
so it is fitting that they are easily swayed.
Jìn, in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, involved the same surname;
with one plot by Lí Jī,
three rulers died because of it,
which is something the world universally grieves.
Tracing the motives of those who acted in this way,
they were blinded by their desire to attain position,
and did not see its difficulty.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* detested their blindness,
so it omitted the words relating to their positions,
and simply spoke of them as the ruler's sons.
As if to say to Xī Qí:
'Alas!
Being the son of a ruler of a great state,
wealth and honor are sufficient,
why covet your brother's position and desire to occupy it,
to have come to this point!'
It recorded words of lament.
Therefore, within sorrow there is greater sorrow:
those who suffered death without guilt,
Shēn Shēng, Xī Qí, and Zhuō Zǐ are examples of this;
among evils, there are evils
that one establishes oneself,
and then one kills oneself.
It is not like other ministers who assassinate their rulers.
Gōngzǐ Shāngrén of Qí is an example of this.
Therefore, the misfortune of Jìn is painful, while the misfortune of Qí is grave.
*Chūnqiū* grieves at the painful and emphasizes the grave.
Therefore, in depriving the son of Jìn of the words of succession,
and in granting the son of Qí the title of ruler,
it details them.
The ancients had a saying:
"If you do not know the future,
look to the past."
Now, the study of the *Chūnqiū*
is to understand the past in order to illuminate the future.
However, its language embodies the subtlety of Heaven,
and is therefore difficult to understand.
If one cannot discern it,
it is as silent as if it did not exist.
If one can discern it,
nothing is left out.
Therefore, those who study the *Chūnqiū*
can grasp one end and connect it to many,
see one opening and penetrate broadly,
then the world is exhausted (understood).
Duke Xī of Lǔ ascended the throne amidst turmoil,
And it was known that he personally entrusted [affairs] to Jìzǐ.
When Jìzǐ was well,
there was no internal disorder among the ministers,
nor external trouble from the feudal lords.
For twenty years,
the state was peaceful and tranquil.
After Jìzǐ passed away,
Lǔ could not withstand the troubles from neighboring states,
and directly begged for troops from Chǔ.
It wasn't that Duke Xī's intentions were entirely unfilial,
but the state became increasingly weak and perilous,
why was this?
Because there was no Jìzǐ.
Because the people of Lǔ were like this,
one also knows that other states are all like this.
Because other states are all like this,
one also knows that the world is all like this.
This is called connecting and threading [it] together.
Therefore, even though the world is large,
and ancient and modern times are long,
it is settled by this.
To employ the worthy is called "the ruler is honored and the state is safe."
wèi zhī zhǔ zūn guó ān.
To employ the wrong person is called "the ruler is debased and the state is endangered."
wèi zhī zhǔ bēi guó wēi,
This is inevitable for all time,
and there is no room for doubt.
It is said in the *Book of Changes*:
「Dǐng zhé zú,
the Duke's gruel is spilled."
Now, "the cauldron's leg is broken" means
entrusting a task to the wrong person;
"the Duke's gruel is spilled" means
the state is overthrown.
Therefore, entrusting a task to the wrong person and the state not being overthrown,
from ancient times to the present, has never been heard of.
Therefore, I examine the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and observe successes and failures,
and I am deeply concerned about the rise and fall of past dynasties.
Employing virtuous ministers
is the rise of the state.
Now, not knowing enough to recognize virtue
is something one can do nothing about.
But knowing virtue yet not being able to employ it,
the great will result in death,
the small will result in disorder and peril.
What can be done about such a situation?
Was it that Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ did not know that Jìzǐ was virtuous?
How else would he, knowing that he was near death, summon and entrust him with the affairs of state?
Was it that Shāng Gōng of Sòng did not know that Kǒng Fù was virtuous?
How else would he, knowing that if Kǒng Fù died, he himself would surely die, hasten to save him?
Both rulers possessed sufficient knowledge to recognize virtue,
but they were indecisive,
and unable to employ it.
Therefore, Lǔ Zhuāng was endangered,
and Sòng Shāng was assassinated.
If Duke Zhuāng had employed Jìzǐ earlier,
Sòng Shāng habitually trusted Kǒng Fù,
and was even about to elevate neighboring states.
How could he merely avoid being murdered!
This is what causes me anxiety and sorrow.
Luxuriant Dew of the Spring and Autumn Annals, Scroll 4
"The Royal Way, Number Six"
Why does the "Spring and Autumn Annals" value the use of "yuán" (元, beginning) in its writing?
"Yuán" means beginning,
implying that the root (foundation) should be correct;
"dào" means the Way of the King;
the King is the origin of the people.
When the King is upright,
then the primordial qi is harmonious and smooth, the wind and rain are timely, auspicious stars appear, and the Yellow Dragon descends;
when the King is not upright,
then Heaven above changes,
and baleful influences appear together.
Under the governance of the Five Emperors and Three Kings,
the world dared not possess [more than a minimal share];
the hearts of the ruler and the people were such that
taxes were only one-tenth.
They were taught with love,
employed with loyalty,
they respected the elders,
treated their relatives with kindness and honored the honorable,
did not deprive the people of their time for agriculture,
and did not require more than three days of service from the people in a year.
The people's families were provided for and had sufficient resources,
There are no worries of resentment and anger, no difficulties of the strong oppressing the weak,
there are no slanderous, treacherous, jealous, or hateful people.
The people cultivate virtue and are beautiful.
They let down their hair, hold food in their mouths, and roam freely.
They do not envy wealth and status.
They are ashamed of evil and do not commit it.
Fathers do not weep for their sons.
Elder brothers do not weep for their younger brothers.
Poisonous insects do not sting.
Fierce beasts do not attack.
Stinging insects do not harm.
Therefore, Heaven sends down sweet dew for them.
Vermilion grass grows.
Sweet springs emerge.
The wind and rain are timely.
Auspicious crops flourish.
Phoenixes and unicorns roam in the suburbs.
The prisons are empty.
Even with beautiful clothing displayed, the people do not commit crimes.
The barbarians from the four directions translate for one another and come to court.
The people's feelings are extremely simple and unadorned.
They sacrifice to Heaven and Earth in the suburbs.
They regulate the mountains and rivers.
At the appropriate time, they proceed to perform the Feng sacrifice on Mount Tài and the Shan sacrifice on Mount Liángfǔ.
They establish the Mingtang (Hall of Light).
They venerate and sacrifice to the deceased emperors.
They match their ancestors with Heaven.
All the lords of the land under Heaven come to offer sacrifices according to their duties.
To offer the ownership of land,
first use it to enter the ancestral temple,
wearing ceremonial cap and robes, then appear before the ancestors.
It is a way of repaying virtue and grace,
and responding to the origin (of things).
Jié and Zhòu, both were descendants of sage kings,
yet they became arrogant, extravagant, and acted recklessly.
They enlarged palaces,
expanded parks and gardens,
exhausted the variations of five colors,
pushed the skill of ornamenting materials to the extreme,
exhausted the feet of wild animals,
drained the resources of mountains and marshes,
and ate beasts of the most evil kinds.
They seized the people's wealth and food,
raised high buildings with carved and engraved decorations,
exhausted the workmanship of gold, jade, bone, and ivory,
enriched the decorations of feathered creatures,
exhausted the variations of black and white,
imposed severe punishments and indulged in random killings to dominate those below,
listened to the music of Zhèng and Wèi,
fulfilled the desires of the collapsing palace,
caged tigers, rhinoceroses, and other beautifully colored beasts,
with the intention of making them rare sights,
rewarded flatterers and bestowed gifts on slanderers.
They made hills from wine dregs,
and made ponds from wine,
Gū pín bù yǎng,
kill sages and dissect their hearts,
burn people alive and smell their stench,
cut open pregnant women to see the transformation (of the fetus),
chop off the feet of those crossing the river in the morning to examine their big toes,
kill Méi Bó and make him into meat paste,
execute the daughter of Guǐ Hóu and take her ring.
Extortion was endless,
the realm was emptied,
the ministers were fearful,
none dared to be fully loyal,
Zhòu became even more self-satisfied.
Zhōu sent out troops,
and those who, without prior agreement, gathered above Méng Jīn,
were eight hundred feudal lords,
who together punished Zhòu,
greatly destroying the realm.
The *Chūn Qiū* takes this as a warning,
saying: "The altar of Bó suffered a disaster."
When Zhōu declined,
the Son of Heaven became weak,
the feudal lords wielded power,
the grand officers controlled the states,
the officers controlled the towns,
they could not practice the proper rituals, laws, and regulations.
The feudal lords rebelled,
none maintained the tribute and exchange,
offering them to the Son of Heaven.
Ministers assassinate their lords,
sons assassinate their fathers,
bastards kill their clan leaders,
they cannot govern properly,
and instead attack and carve each other up to expand their territories.
They use the strong to coerce each other,
and cannot control their subordinates.
The strong swallow the weak,
the many oppress the few,
the rich exploit the poor,
and annexation continues without end.
Inferiors overstep their superiors,
and they cannot be stopped.
The sun suffers an eclipse,
stars fall like rain,
locusts rain down,
sandy deer collapse (or a sandy deer mountain collapses),
in summer, there are great floods,
in winter, there are great snowfalls,
five stones fall in Sòng,
six seabirds fly backwards,
falling frost does not kill the grass,
plums and prunes bear fruit,
the first month is without rain,
until the seventh month of autumn,
there is an earthquake,
Mount Liáng collapses,
blocking the river,
For three days the water did not flow,
the daytime was dark,
a comet appeared in the east,
and rushed towards the constellation Dà Chén.
Storks and mynas came to nest,
the *Chūnqiū* considered this strange,
using it to show signs of disobedience and disorder.
Kǒngzǐ clearly distinguished gains and losses,
differentiated nobility and inferiority,
and returned to the fundamentals of the Way of the King.
He criticized the King of Heaven to bring about great peace.
He criticized evil and ridiculed the subtle,
omitting nothing great or small.
He promoted good even if it was trivial,
and eliminated evil even if it was slight.
Promoting good and punishing evil,
cuts off everything at its source.
The King of Heaven sent Zǎi Xuān to return the gifts presented at the funeral of Duke Huì's son Zhòngzǐ;
this criticized being untimely.
The King of Heaven attacked Zhèng,
this criticized being too familiar.
He met with the King's heir apparent,
this criticized being too subtle.
Jì Gōng came to welcome the Queen back,
this criticized a breach of etiquette.
He criticized Jiā Fù for requesting carriages,
Wǔshì Máo Bó for requesting funeral money,
The king sent men to rescue Wèi.
The royal army was defeated at Mào Róng.
The Heavenly King was not supported.
He went out and resided in Zhèng.
He killed his half-brother.
The royal house was in chaos.
It could not extend its influence abroad.
It was divided into Eastern and Western Zhōu.
It had no way to lead the world.
He summoned the Marquis of Wèi.
He could not bring him.
He sent Zǐ Tū to attack Wèi.
He could not cut it off.
He attacked Zhèng.
He could not make them submit.
Wú hài destroyed Jí.
He could not punish them.
The feudal lords were able to cause great disorder.
Usurpations and assassinations never ceased.
Subordinates oppressed their superiors.
They presumptuously imitated the Son of Heaven.
The strong feudal lords exercised their power.
Small states were destroyed.
Jìn went so far as to invade Zhōu three times.
He fought with the Heavenly King at Mào Róng.
And greatly defeated him.
The Róng captured Fán Bó at Chǔ Qiū.
And took him back.
The feudal lords were originally resentful and followed evil,
dispatching troops to attack each other,
destroying people’s ancestral temples and altars,
and were unable to govern properly.
Ministers and sons became powerful
to the point of murdering their lords and fathers.
Laws and regulations were abandoned,
and were no longer used.
Authority was cut off,
and was no longer exercised.
Therefore, Zhèng and Lǔ exchanged lands,
Duke Wén of Jìn twice installed the Son of Heaven,
Duke Huán of Qí met with the heir of the king,
and arbitrarily enfeoffed Xíng, Wèi, and Qǐ,
running rampant in the Central States,
intending to rule the world.
Lǔ performed the eight-row dance,
sacrificed to Mount Tài in the north,
and made suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
doing what only the Son of Heaven should do.
Because of these things,
thirty-two rulers were murdered,
and fifty-two states were destroyed.
This was caused by the failure to stop small evils.
The "Spring and Autumn Annals" establishes the principle that:
the Son of Heaven sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
the feudal lords sacrifice to the altars of soil and grain,
The mountains and rivers that are not within the fief are not to be sacrificed to.
When the Son of Heaven exists,
the feudal lords must not independently control land,
must not independently grant fiefs,
must not independently employ the Son of Heaven's grand officers,
must not perform the Son of Heaven's music,
must not deliver the Son of Heaven's taxes,
must not associate with the Son of Heaven's nobles.
No one should lead the ruler's personal troops;
if they do, they shall be punished.
Grand officers must not have hereditary positions,
and grand officers must not disregard or set aside the ruler's commands.
In establishing the heir,
precedence is given to seniority, not to virtue;
in establishing a son (as heir), precedence is given to noble birth, not to seniority.
In establishing the principal wife, precedence is given to the proper wife, not to a concubine.
The Son of Heaven does not treat the relatives of the empress mother as subjects;
one draws near those who are close in order to bring in those who are distant.
Therefore, there has never been a case of not first drawing near those who are close and then bringing in those who are distant.
Therefore, one prioritizes his own state and regards the other states of the Xia as external,
one prioritizes the states of the Xia and regards the Yi and Di (barbarian tribes) as external;
speech begins from what is closest.
The feudal lords who come to court are praised.
Yífǔ of Zhū Lóu is allowed to use a courtesy name.
Téng and Xuē are addressed as marquis.
Jīng gains personnel.
Jiè Gélú gains a name.
What is said internally (at court) is called "as."
When the feudal lords come, it is called an "audience" (朝, cháo).
When the grand masters come, it is called a "visit" (聘, pìn).
This is the idea of the kingly way.
Punishing evil must not overlook the small or the great.
The feudal lords must not raise armies for commoners.
They must not arrest the grand masters of the Son of Heaven.
Arresting the grand masters of the Son of Heaven
is the same crime as attacking a state.
Arresting Fán Bó is declared an attack.
Presenting eight rows (of dancers),
one avoids saying "eight" and says "six."
When Zhèng and Lǔ exchanged lands,
one avoids saying "exchange" and says "borrow."
When Jìn Wén twice summoned the Son of Heaven,
one avoids saying "summon" and says "hunt."
Duke Huán preserved Xíng, Wèi, and Qǐ,
which is not found in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
One approves of the action in one's heart,
but the law cuts it off and does not allow it.
This is the way to stop chaos;
it is not what the feudal lords should do.
According to the meaning of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
a minister who does not punish a traitor
is not a minister.
A son who does not avenge (his father)
is not a son.
Therefore, punishing Zhào Dùn, whose traitor was not punished,
Not recording the burial [of someone] indicates the punishment of a subject or son.
Xǔ Shìzǐ Zhǐ (許世子止) not tasting the medicine [for his father]
and being punished as a patricide;
Chǔ Gōngzǐ Bǐ (楚公子比) being coerced into ascending the throne,
yet not escaping death;
Qí Huán (齊桓) and Jìn Wén (晉文) presumptuously enfeoffing [others],
[thereby] manipulating the Son of Heaven,
terminating lineages, continuing lineages, preserving the fallen,
launching invasions, holding assemblies—
always acting as the primary authority.
It is said:
"Duke Huán (桓公) rescued the central states
and repelled the barbarian tribes;
eventually subjugated Chǔ (楚),
thus achieving the affairs of a true king."
Duke Wén of Jìn (晉文) restored the Son of Heaven a second time.
All of these actions, however, were not punished,
[because the *Chūnqiū*] praised their leadership of the feudal lords
and their dedication to offering tribute to the Son of Heaven and restoring the House of Zhōu (周).
The *Chūnqiū* recognized them as hegemons.
This is what is meant by punishing the intention, not the wording.
Lǔ Yǐn (魯隱) replacing Duke Huán (桓) to stand [as ruler],
Jì Zhòng (祭仲)'s ousting [of Duke] Hū (忽) and establishing [Duke] Tū (突),
the martyrdom of Chóu Mù (仇牧), Kǒng Fù (孔父), and Xún Xī (荀息),
Gōngzǐ Mù Yí (公子目夷) not siding with the state of Chǔ (楚)
these all seized authority to preserve the state,
To practice the righteousness of the world,
to maintain a sincere heart,
the *Spring and Autumn Annals* praises such qi and righteousness,
therefore all are recorded,
which is called restoration to correctness.
The barbarians Zhūlóu people, Móu people, Gé people,
were criticized for their kings' deaths leading to mutual visits and embassies,
this is their punishment.
Killing the heir apparent and the younger brother by the same mother,
and directly claiming the title of ruler,
clearly shows the loss of kinship.
Lǔ Jìzǐ's exemption from punishment,
and Wú Jìzǐ's relinquishment of the state,
demonstrate the kindness of kinship.
The gatekeeper killing Wú Zǐ Yújì,
shows that those who commit crimes should not be approached.
Zhèng Bó Kūnwán died during a meeting,
the killing is omitted,
lamenting that powerful ministers dominate the ruler,
so the ruler cannot do good.
The people of Wèi killed Zhōu Xū,
the people of Qí killed Wúzhī,
illustrating the righteousness between ruler and minister,
and upholding the correctness of the state.
The people of Wèi establishing Jìn,
praises gaining the support of the people.
The ruler will not speak of leading the army,
emphasizing the righteousness of the ruler.
In the first month,
the Duke was in Chu,
the ministers and sons missed their lord,
not a single day passed without thoughts of the lord.
Punishing those who received orders,
thinking of Wèi Bǎo,
was to correct the fairness of the prison.
The record of the siege of Chéng,
the Jiawu sacrifice to the soldiers,
was to distinguish the crime of coercion,
and punish the law of intent.
Building the South Gate,
carved rafters,
red pillars,
building the pheasant gate and two towers,
constructing three terraces,
newly extended stables,
was to criticize arrogance, extravagance, and disregard for those below.
Therefore, Zāngsūn Chén requested to purchase grain from Qi,
Confucius said:
"A gentleman governing a state,
must have three years of reserves,
if one year is not productive,
only then should he request to purchase grain,
this is a failure of the lord's duty."
Punishing those who initiate offenses,
reducing punishments and eliminating evil,
is to hate the beginning.
Dàfū (大夫) made a covenant at Chányuān (澶淵),
criticizing the exclusive power of the dàfū.
When the feudal lords gathered,
the virtuous ones were the leaders,
honoring virtue.
The *Chūnqiū* (春秋) records even the slightest errors,
reflecting on the way of the king,
valuing trust and returning to the ancient ways,
simply settling matters with words,
not resorting to sacrificial covenants to finalize agreements.
Therefore, it says:
"The Marquis of Qí (齊侯) and the Marquis of Wèi (衛侯) mutually exchanged mandates at Pú (蒲)."
The *Commentary* says:
"In ancient times, covenants were not made,
agreements were concluded with words, and then they withdrew."
Sòng Bó Jī (宋伯姬) said:
"A woman does not go out at night,
and if her chaperone is not present,
she does not leave the hall."
It is said:
"In ancient times, when the Duke of Zhōu (周公) campaigned in the east,
the western states resented it."
Duke Huán (桓公) said:
"Do not hoard grain,
do not block valleys,
do not easily plant trees for profit,
do not make a concubine a wife."
Duke Xiāng of Sòng (宋襄公) said:
"Do not advance to form ranks if the drums are not sounded,
and do not corner others."
Zhuāng Wáng said:
"In ancient times, if a wooden vessel was not cracked,
and the leather was not moth-eaten,
it was not taken out [of storage]."
A junzi is steadfast in propriety,
and indifferent to profit;
he values the person,
and not their land;
he does not pardon those who inform [on others],
which is inauspicious;
the strong do not bully the weak.
Qí Qǐnggōng visited the dead and inquired after the sick;
Kǒng Fǔ stood upright and with a stern expression in the court,
and no one dared to go beyond him to present difficulties to their ruler;
Qí Guózhuǒ did not disgrace his lord's commands,
and respected the Marquis of Qí;
this is the "Spring and Autumn Annals" saving the embellishment with substance.
Saving embellishment with substance,
one can see therein how the various lords of the world lost their states; it is also contained therein.
The Viscount of Lù wished to unite the rites and righteousness of the Central States,
and distance himself from the barbarian tribes,
but he did not conform to the standards of the Central States,
and therefore he perished.
King Fūchāi of Wú exerted his strength against Yuè,
treating the lords of others as his vassals,
and taking the wives of others as his concubines,
In the end, he perished himself,
his ancestral temple was razed,
and his altars of soil and grain were destroyed.
How lamentable!
King Chang cast himself into death.
Alas!
Is this not sorrowful!
The conduct of Líng of Jìn was without propriety,
he stayed on a terrace
and shot at his courtiers with pellets.
He dismembered cooks and threw them away.
He divulged the plot of Yáng Chǔfǔ,
causing Yáng Chǔfǔ to die.
And when he was troubled by the remonstrances of Zhào Dùn,
he wanted to kill him.
In the end, he was killed by Zhào Chuān.
Duke Xiàn of Jìn acted contrary to reason,
killing the heir apparent, Shēnshēng,
and with Lí Jī established Xīqí and Zhuōzǐ.
They were all killed.
The state fell into great disorder,
and only after four generations was it stabilized.
It almost was destroyed by Qín,
all originating from Lí Jī.
King Píng of Chǔ acted without restraint,
killing the father and elder brother of Wǔ Zǐxū.
Duke Zhāo of Cài went to court to him
and thereupon requested his fur coat.
Duke Zhāo did not agree,
The King of Wú criticized him,
Raised troops to attack Chǔ,
Greatly defeated them,
The ruler lodged in the ruler's chambers,
The grand masters lodged in the grand master's chambers,
He took the mother of the King of Chǔ as his wife,
This was brought about by greed and tyranny.
Duke Lì of Jìn practiced tyrannical ways,
Killed innocent people,
In one morning he killed three high officials,
The next year,
His ministers were fearful and apprehensive,
The state of Jìn killed him.
Marquis Tuó of Chén was licentious in Cài,
The people of Cài killed him.
In ancient times, when the feudal lords went beyond their borders, they had to have attendants on their left and right,
And be prepared with a military force,
In order to prepare for the unexpected.
Now, Marquis Tuó of Chén freely entered and exited among the common people in person,
And died at the hands of commoners in his neighborhood,
This is very much not the conduct of a ruler.
Duke Mǐn of Sòng cherished women and was jealous in his heart,
And gambled with the grand master Wàn.
Wàn praised Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ, saying:
"Among all the feudal lords in the land, the one who is suitable to be a ruler,
Is only Marquis Lǔ."
Duke Mǐn was jealous of his words,
He said:
"These are captives.
You captive,
how would you know the good or bad of the Marquis of Lǔ?"
Sòng Wàn became angry,
grappled with Duke Mǐn,
severed his head.
This was the fault of playing a game as equals with a subject.
In ancient times, the ruler stood in the shade,
and the ministers stood in the sun;
this was to distinguish positions
and make clear the noble and the base.
Now, playing a game face to face with a subject,
and placing women on the side,
this is to have no distinction between ruler and subject.
Therefore, he caused Wàn to praise other countries,
to belittle the intention of Duke Mǐn.
Duke Mǐn reproached Wàn,
and personally played a game with him.
A base ruler demeans himself,
has insulted the women's chambers,
together showing off the women,
and uniquely obtains the path to being killed.
The *Chūnqiū Zhuàn* says:
"A minister does not come close to the ruler."
To stay far away is to avoid being too close.
The state of Liáng internally conscripted the people without end,
its people could not bear it,
To make the people group themselves into fives according to location,
if one family flees,
the other four families are punished with death.
The people say:
"Those who flee first are rewarded,
those who flee later are punished."
A ruler
should seek to make the people filial to their parents,
obedient to their elders,
guard the burial mounds,
maintain the ancestral temples,
and generation after generation sacrifice to their ancestors.
Now, seeking wealth is never enough,
carrying out punishments is like not being able to win,
and slaughter is like butchering.
He makes his people enemies,

*Tōng Guó Shēn Dì Èrshí'èr* (Chapter Twenty-Two, "Governing the Body in a Universal Nation")
The purest part of *qì* is essence (*jīng*).
The purest part of people is virtue (*xián*).
One who governs the body uses virtue (*xián*),
accumulating essence (*jīng*) as treasure.
One who governs a nation uses accumulated virtue (*xián*) as the proper way.
The body takes the mind as its foundation.
The state takes the ruler as its master.
If essence (*jīng*) accumulates at its foundation,
then blood and *qì* mutually support each other.
If virtue (*xián*) accumulates in its master,
then superiors and inferiors mutually restrain and employ each other.
If blood and *qì* mutually support each other,
then the body will have no suffering.
If superiors and inferiors mutually restrain and employ each other,
then the various officials will each obtain their proper place.
If the body has no suffering,
then the body can be secured and made tranquil.
When the hundred officials each obtain their proper positions,
only then can the state be secured and defended.
Now, if one wishes to attain refinement,
one must make one's form empty and tranquil.
If one wishes to attract the worthy,
one must make one's person humble and unassuming.
When the form is tranquil and the will is empty,
it is where refined *qì* tends to go.
Humbling oneself and esteeming lowliness,
is what the benevolent and worthy attend to.
Therefore, in governing oneself,
one must strive to hold to emptiness and tranquility in order to attain refinement.
In governing a state,
one must strive to be completely humble and unassuming in order to attract the worthy.
If one is able to attain refinement,
then one will combine enlightenment and longevity.
If benevolence can attract the worthy,
then virtuous grace will be abundant and the state will be at great peace.

What the "Spring and Autumn Annals" governs,
is people and me;
that which governs people and me,
is benevolence and righteousness;
use benevolence to pacify people,
use righteousness to rectify myself;
Therefore, the meaning of "rén" 仁 is "person" (rén 人).
The meaning of "yì" 義 is "I" (wǒ 我).
These are names used to distinguish them.
"Rén" in relation to others,
and "yì" in relation to oneself,
must be carefully examined.
The masses do not understand this,
and thus, on the contrary, enrich themselves with "rén,"
while using "yì" to impose on others.
They distort their position and go against the principles;
it is rare for there not to be disorder.
Therefore, no one desires disorder,
but for the most part, disorder constantly occurs.
This is all because they are ignorant of the distinction between "others" and "self,"
and do not understand where "rén" and "yì" truly lie.
Therefore, the *Chūnqiū* 春秋 is the standard for "rén" and "yì."
The standard of "rén" lies in loving others,
not in loving oneself.
The standard of "yì" lies in correcting oneself,
not in correcting others.
If I do not correct myself,
even if I can correct others,
it will not be considered "yì."
If others are not blessed by one's love,
even if one loves oneself deeply,
it will not be considered "rén."
In the past,

However, the reason he cannot be considered a virtuous person is that

Examine his love based on the people.
Down to birds, beasts, insects, and crawling creatures, there is none that he loves.
If he does not love,

Benevolence is the name for loving others.
Regarding Xī (酅),

He himself went in pursuit

The army had already been deployed against them

To save early and act in advance,

Thus, observing the movement of things,

cutting off chaos and blocking harm at the time when they are about to happen but have not yet acted,

Its clarity is ultimate.

Generally, love only extends to oneself.
Therefore, it is said:
the benevolent love others,

The meaning of righteousness,

Even in chaotic times with twisted superiors,

What is meant by righteousness!

righteousness lies in correcting oneself,
It does not lie in the upright person;
this is its method.
If I lack something and seek it from others,

The principle is contrary!
How can this be called *yì* (righteousness/appropriateness)?
*Yì* means what is appropriate to me.
What is appropriate to me,

Therefore, when speaking of *yì*,

By applying this,

those who act and lose *yì*,

Comparing with this,

Thus, *yì* and *rén* (benevolence/humanity) are different.
Benevolence means going forth,

Benevolence is very far,

Love residing in others is called benevolence,

Benevolence is master of others,

Therefore, in governing internally, one reverses principle to rectify the self,

First his work,

The *Spring and Autumn Annals* criticizes the faults of superiors,

all these six things,

"Must be Benevolent and Wise, Number Thirty"
Nothing is closer than benevolence,
nothing is more urgent than wisdom.
If one is not benevolent but has courage, strength, talent, and ability,
then they are like a madman wielding a sharp weapon;
if one is not wise but is eloquent, clever, and quick-witted,
then they are like someone lost riding a fine horse.
Therefore, if one is neither benevolent nor wise but possesses talent and ability,
they will use their talent and ability to assist their wicked and狂 (xiékuáng) heart,
and praise their deviant and rebellious actions,
which will only magnify their errors and worsen their evil.
Their strength is sufficient to cover up faults,
their resistance is sufficient to commit fraud,
their cleverness is sufficient to deceive the foolish,
their eloquence is sufficient to embellish wrongs,
their firmness is sufficient to decisively act perversely,
their sternness is sufficient to reject remonstrance.
This is not a lack of talent and ability,
but their application is improper and their conduct is unjust.
Those who have a rebellious heart
should not be given convenient power,
those who are inherently foolish should not be given sharp tools.
What the *Lún* 論
calls "not knowing people"
likely refers to not being able to distinguish these kinds of people.
If one is benevolent but lacks knowledge,
then one loves without discernment.
If one has knowledge but lacks benevolence,
Therefore, the benevolent person is one who loves humankind,
and the wise person is one who removes its harm.
What is called benevolence?
The benevolent person is compassionate and loves others,
is cautious and harmonious, and does not contend,
has clear and respectful preferences,
has no harmful or malicious thoughts,
has no hidden or secretive intentions,
has no envious or jealous temperament,
has no feelings of sorrow or desire,
has no treacherous or biased actions,
has no evasive or disobedient conduct.
Therefore, their heart is at ease,
their intentions are peaceful,
their temperament is harmonious,
their desires are restrained,
their affairs are easy to manage,
and their conduct is aligned with the Way.
Thus, they are able to be peaceful, easygoing, harmonious, and reasonable without contention.
Such a person is called benevolent.
What is meant by knowledge?
It is speaking first and then being correct.
Whenever people want to abandon conduct,
they all use their knowledge to plan first and then act.
If their planning is correct,
then what they do succeeds,
their affairs are proper,
their conduct is accomplished,
their name is honored,
their person benefits greatly and has no worries,
blessings extend to their children and grandchildren,
virtue is added to all the people;
Tāng and Wǔ are examples of this.
If their planning is incorrect,
then what they do does not succeed in their affairs,
their affairs are not proper,
their conduct is not accomplished,
their name is disgraced,
harm reaches their person,
their line is cut off without restoration,
their clan is destroyed, their lineage extinguished, and their country perishes, such as these.
Therefore, it is said:
Nothing is more urgent than knowledge.
The knowledgeable see misfortune and fortune far in advance,
they know benefit and harm early,
when things move, they know their transformations,
when matters arise, they know their destination,
seeing the beginning, they know the end,
To speak it, and none dare to make a clamor;
to establish it, and it cannot be discarded;
to take it up, and it cannot be relinquished;
the beginning and the end do not contradict each other;
the end and the beginning are of the same kind;
to contemplate it, and there is a return;
to reach it, and one cannot be satiated.
Its words are few and sufficient,
concise and illustrative,
simple and expressive,
sparing and complete,
so little that nothing can be added,
so much that nothing can be subtracted;
its actions accord with moral principles,
its words address urgent matters.
Such a person is called wise.
The general categories of these are such:
among the things of Heaven and Earth, there are those that undergo unusual changes,
which are called anomalies (yì);
the smaller ones are called disasters (zāi).
Disasters always arrive first, and anomalies then follow them.
Disasters are Heaven's reproaches;
anomalies are Heaven's majesty.
When reproached and not knowing,
then one is intimidated with majesty.
The *Shī* says,
"Fear the majesty of Heaven."
This is probably what it means.
The root of all calamities and anomalies
entirely arises from the faults of the state.
When the faults of the state first begin to sprout,
Heaven sends down calamities to reprimand and warn it.
If reprimanded and warned, yet it does not know to change,
then strange anomalies are seen to frighten and alarm it.
If frightened and alarmed, yet it still does not know to be fearful and apprehensive,
then its calamities and faults will reach their culmination.
From this, we can see that Heaven's intent is benevolent and does not wish to ensnare people.
We respectfully observe:
Calamities and anomalies reveal the will of Heaven.
Heaven's will has desires and aversions.
What it desires and what it does not desire,
people should examine within themselves,
and there should be a chastening in their hearts.
Outwardly, they should observe affairs,
and there should be verification within the state.
Therefore, those who understand Heaven's will in calamities and anomalies,
fear them but do not resent them,
believing that Heaven wishes to correct our faults,
and save us from our errors,
therefore, it repays us in this way.
According to the principles of the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
when superiors alter the ancient ways and change the norms,
and celestial disasters occur in response to this,
it is called a "fortunate country."
Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) said:
"What Heaven favors
is to repeatedly bring calamity to those who do evil."
Moreover, King Zhuang said:
"Heaven does not show disasters,
the earth does not show calamities."
Then he prayed to the mountains and rivers,
saying:
"Is Heaven going to destroy me!
Not pointing out my faults,
but maximizing my sins."
From this perspective,
heavenly disasters arrive in response to faults,
the manifestation of anomalies is clearly fearsome.
This is what Heaven wants to save,
and what the *Spring and Autumn Annals* uniquely favors,
which is why King Zhuang prayed and requested.
Even a sage ruler and virtuous lord are pleased to receive remonstrations from loyal ministers,
how much more so should they accept heavenly reprimands?
*Luxuriant Dew of the Spring and Autumn Annals*, Scroll 9
"Nourishing the Body is Secondary to Righteousness, Section Thirty-One"
Heaven's creation of people
causes them to generate righteousness and profit;
profit to nourish their body,
righteousness to nourish their mind.
If the mind does not obtain righteousness, it cannot be happy;
if the body does not obtain profit, it cannot be at peace.
Righteousness is the nourishment of the mind,
Profit is what nourishes the body.
Nothing is more valuable to the body than the mind,
therefore, nothing is more important to nurture than righteousness.
The way righteousness nourishes life is greater than profit.
How do we know this?
Nowadays, there are people who possess great righteousness but very little profit.
Even though they are poor and humble,
they can still accommodate their actions,
and find pleasure in themselves and joy in living.
Examples include people like Yuán Xiàn, Zēng (probably referring to Zēng Shēn), and Mǐn (probably referring to Mǐn Zǐqiān).
There are people who have great profit but are greatly devoid of righteousness.
Even though they are very wealthy,
they experience great shame and disgrace.
When evil is deep,
calamities are severe,
and if they do not immediately die for their crimes,
they will soon be hurt by misfortune and sorrow.
They cannot live happily and complete their lives.
Such are the people who are punished by execution and die prematurely.
Indeed, a person who has righteousness,
even if poor, can be happy;
but one who is greatly without righteousness,
even if rich, cannot sustain himself.
I therefore truly believe that righteousness nourishes life,
being greater than profit and more substantial than wealth.
The people cannot understand this,
and they constantly act contrary to it.
They all forget righteousness and pursue profit,
去理而走邪，
以賊其身而禍其家。 To depart from principle and pursue wickedness is to injure oneself and bring calamity upon one's family.
此非其自為計不忠也，
則其知之所不能明也。 This is not because their plans for themselves are disloyal; rather, it is because their understanding cannot discern clearly.
今握棗與錯金，
以示嬰兒，
嬰兒必取棗而不取金也。 If one now holds a jujube date and inlaid gold, and shows them to an infant, the infant will surely take the jujube date and not take the gold.
握一斤金與千萬之珠，
以示野人，
野人必取金而不取珠也。 If one holds a pound of gold and millions of pearls, and shows them to a rustic, the rustic will surely take the gold and not take the pearls.
故物之於人，
小者易知也，
其於大者難見也。 Therefore, regarding things as they relate to people, the small ones are easily understood, while the large ones are difficult to see.
今利之於人小而義之於人大者，
無怪民之皆趨利而不趨義也，

固其所闇也。 Now, profit is small in relation to people, while righteousness is large in relation to people. It is no wonder that the people all pursue profit and do not pursue righteousness; it is inherently what they are blind to.
聖人事明義，
以照燿其所闇，
故民不陷。 The sage makes it his business to clarify righteousness, in order to illuminate what they are blind to, therefore the people do not fall into traps.
《詩》云：
「示我顯德行。」
此之謂也。 The *Classic of Poetry* says, "Show us the manifest virtues." This is what it means.
先王顯德以示民，
民樂而歌之以為詩，
說而化之以為俗。 The former kings manifested virtue to show the people, the people rejoiced and sang of it, taking it as poetry, delighted and transformed it into customs.
故不令而自行，
不禁而自止，
從上之意，
It does not require being made to do it;
it is as if it is natural.
Therefore, it is said:
That the sage moves Heaven and Earth and transforms the four seasons,
it is not because of anything else;
it is because his understanding of righteousness is great that he can move things,
he moves things, so he can transform them,
he transforms them, so he can greatly implement things,
he transforms and greatly implements things, so laws are not violated,
laws are not violated, so punishments are not used,
if punishments are not used, then it is the merit of Yáo and Shùn.
This is the way of great order,
transmitted and restored by the former sages.
Therefore, Confucius said:
"Who can go out without going through the door?
Why not follow this way!"
Now, if you do not demonstrate manifest virtue,
the people will be ignorant of righteousness
and unable to see;
confused about the Way and unable to understand,
therefore, you want to use great severity and harshness to surely correct them,
this would directly injure and harm the people of Heaven and diminish the virtue of the ruler;
this approach will not work.
Zhòngní said:
"If the state has the Way,
even if punishments are added,
there is no punishment.
If the state has no Way,
Even if you kill them,
you cannot overcome them."
The so-called having or not having the Way
refers to showing or not showing manifest virtuous conduct.
"Reply to the King of Jiaoxi on Why One Cannot Consider the Grand Masters of Yue Benevolent, Number Thirty-Two"
The commanding minister said:
"Grand Master Lí, Grand Master Zhǒng, Grand Master Yōng, Grand Master Gāo, Grand Master Chē Chéng,
the King of Yue consulted with these five grand masters about attacking Wu,
and consequently destroyed it,
wiping away the shame of Kuàijī,
and ultimately became a hegemon.
Fàn Lǐ left him,
Zhǒng died for him.
I consider both of these grand masters to be virtuous.
Confucius said,
'Yin had three men of benevolence.'
Now, considering the virtue of the King of Yue,
and the abilities of Lí and Zhǒng,
these three men,
I also consider Yue to have three men of benevolence.
What do you think about this, sir?
Duke Huan resolved his doubts by consulting with Guǎn Zhòng;
I resolve my doubts by consulting with you."
Zhòngshū prostrated himself on the ground and bowed twice,
replying,
"Zhòngshū's knowledge is limited and his learning is shallow,
insufficient to resolve this.
Although,
if the ruler has questions for his subject,
your subject dares not but answer in full,
this is proper etiquette.
Your subject, Zhòng Shū, has heard:
In the past,
the Lord of Lǔ asked Liǔ Xiàhuì, saying:
"I wish to attack Qí,
what do you think?"
Liǔ Xiàhuì replied,
"It is not permissible."
He withdrew and wore a worried expression,
saying,
"I have heard it said,
those who plan to attack a state
do not ask a person of benevolence.
Why did it come to me?"
He only saw being asked and was already ashamed of it,
how much more so to participate in deceit to attack Wú!
It is clearly inappropriate.
Viewing it from this perspective,
Yuè fundamentally has no one benevolent person,
so how could they obtain three benevolent people!
A person of benevolence
straightens their path and does not scheme for profit,
cultivates their principles and does not rush for accomplishments,
achieves non-action and customs are greatly transformed,
such a person can be called benevolent and sage.
These are the Three Kings.
The meaning of the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) is to
value trustworthiness and despise deceit.
To deceive people and then defeat them,
even if there is merit,
a gentleman will not do it.
Therefore, in the school of Zhòng Ní
even a five-foot-tall child
would be ashamed to mention the Five Hegemons.
Because they used deceit to achieve success,
doing anything as long as it worked,
they are not worthy of mention in the school of the great gentlemen.
The Five Hegemons,
compared to other feudal lords, were considered virtuous,
but compared to the benevolent and virtuous,
what virtue did they have?
It is like wǔfū being compared to beautiful jade.
Your subject Zhòng Shū kowtows again to report this."

*Shēn Chá Míng Hào Dì Sān Shí Wǔ* (Chapter Thirty-Five: Profoundly Examining Names and Titles)
The key to governing the world
lies in carefully distinguishing the great.
The key to distinguishing the great
lies in profoundly examining names and titles.
Names are the primary chapter of great principles.
Recording the meaning of this primary chapter
in order to glimpse the matters within,
then right and wrong can be known,
and rebellion and obedience will naturally become clear,
its workings will then extend throughout Heaven and Earth.
The correctness of right and wrong
is derived from rebellion and obedience;
the correctness of rebellion and obedience
is derived from names and titles;
the correctness of names and titles
is derived from Heaven and Earth;
Tiāndì are used as the grand meaning of titles and names.
The ancient sages,
emulated Tiāndì through imitation, calling it "hào" (號, title);
and conveyed mandates through pronouncements, calling it "míng" (名, name).
"Míng" as a term means to proclaim and to mandate.
"Hào" as a term means to emulate through imitation.
To emulate Tiāndì through imitation is "hào".
To proclaim and mandate is "míng".
Names and titles have different sounds but the same origin,
both being pronouncements and imitations to express the will of Heaven.
Heaven does not speak,
but causes people to express its intent;
it does not act directly,
but causes people to carry out its will.
Names, then, are the expression of Heaven's will by the sages,
and must be deeply considered.
The ruler who receives the Mandate
is the one favored by Heaven's will.
Therefore, he who is titled "Tiānzǐ" (天子, Son of Heaven)
should regard Heaven as his father,
and serve Heaven with filial piety.
He who is titled "zhūhóu" (諸侯, feudal lord)
should carefully regard the Tiānzǐ whom he awaits and serves.
He who is titled "dàfū" (大夫, high official)
should deepen his loyalty and trustworthiness,
cultivate his propriety and righteousness,
making his goodness greater than that of commoners,
so that it is sufficient to transform others.
"Shì" means affairs,
"mín" means ignorance;
if the "shì" do not attain transformation,
they can only be made to guard affairs and follow their superiors.
The five designations commend themselves,
each having its own division.
Within the divisions are subtleties,
and the subtleties have names.
Names are numerous compared to designations,
designations encompass their entirety.
What is meant by "name"
is naming their separation and dispersal.
Designations are general and brief,
names are detailed and specific.
"Specific" means widely distinguishing their affairs,
"general" means singly raising their great affairs.
Paying respect to ghosts and spirits is designated,
one is called "jì" (sacrifice).
The scattered names of "jì,"
in spring it is called "cí,"
in summer it is called "yuè,"
in autumn it is called "cháng,"

Hunting birds and beasts is designated,
one is called "tián" (field/hunt).
The scattered names of "tián,"
in spring it is "miáo,"
in autumn it is "sōu,"
Winter hunt,
summer hunt.

All things have general names,

The interaction between Heaven and humanity
is united as one.
Alike and connected in principle,
acting to benefit each other,
compliant and receptive to each other,
